title: Evaluate-and-Repair for LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes: A Preregistered Generate–Verify–Repair Study with a Deterministic Net Verifier
abstract: We report a preregistered, fully autonomous experiment that evaluated whether a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline—where an LLM proposes device-level configuration changes and a deterministic network verifier gates acceptance and supplies failure diagnostics for automated repair—reduces the acceptance of unsafe or policy‑violating NetOps changes in a seeded NetOps sandbox. Design (preregistered): paired within‑task comparison on N=300 canonical device‑level tasks (routing 150 / ACL 100 / BGP 50) using gpt‑5‑mini as the proposer; conditions: LLM‑only (baseline) and guarded GVR (deterministic verifier gate + up to one repair iteration). Primary estimand: paired difference in the proportion of proposals that would cause an unsafe sandbox state if applied. Results (confirmatory): complete pairs = 300; unsafe‑would‑occur proposals: baseline = 1/300 (0.33%), guarded = 0/300 (0.00%); paired absolute risk reduction = 0.0033 (95% CI 0.000–0.01, McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00). The preregistered claims H1/H2 (substantial reduction, ≥50%) are not supported; the observed reduction is numerically small and statistically null under the preregistered test. Exploratory diagnostics show: (i) very high baseline safety for these canonical tasks, (ii) the single discordant case was corrected by the repair loop when supplied verifier counterexamples, and (iii) remaining failures are concentrated in subtle reachability-policy interactions beyond the verifier’s modeled policy scope. We discuss operational implications, construct/internal/external validity threats, and reproducibility artifacts (all prompts, raw outputs, verifier traces, scoring artifacts, and hashes are archived).

sections.introduction: Modern NetOps workflows are beginning to use LLMs to translate operator intent into device configurations or change plans. However, the stochastic generation dynamic of LLMs conflicts with the zero‑defect requirements of production network changes. The Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pattern interposes deterministic verification oracles between probabilistic generation and acceptance to constrain outputs to a verifiable correct subset; analogous approaches have been proposed for regulated code generation and other high‑assurance domains. This work asks: does a GVR pipeline with a deterministic net verifier materially reduce the rate of unsafe device‑level proposals compared with LLM proposals alone, under a constrained, preregistered NetOps sandbox? We answer this with a fully preregistered, reproducible, paired experiment run end‑to‑end by the autonomous researcher. Contributions: (1) a preregistered confirmatory experiment (N=300) comparing baseline LLM proposals to a verifier‑gated GVR pipeline using gpt‑5‑mini; (2) a complete public execution manifest and analysis artifacts (prompts, raw outputs, verifier counterexamples, repair context, and hashes); (3) empirical finding that, for the canonical seeded task set, baseline unsafe proposals were already rare (1/300) and the gated GVR arm reduced unsafe proposals to 0/300 but without statistical significance for the preregistered effect-size target; (4) an evidence‑rooted discussion of failure modes and evaluation limitations to guide subsequent NetOps GVR research.
sections.related_work: Relevant prior work spans (i) generate‑verify‑repair architectures in code and regulated domains, (ii) deterministic network verification and reachability analysis, and (iii) agentic NetOps design patterns that emphasise contracts, bounded tools, and canary/rollback evaluation. Representative verified sources used for positioning and protocol design: Cadenas (Convergent Correctness / GVR conceptualization) described a layered GVR approach for stochastic code generation (ssrn:6754899); retrieval‑augmented generation and grounding methods survey the limits of grounding alone for operational safety (Gao et al., arXiv:2312.10997); SymNet and related data‑plane symbolic/semantic verification tools demonstrate practical deterministic analyses for forwarding/reachability properties (Stoenescu et al., SIGCOMM 2016). NetOps/AIOps surveys emphasise assurance contracts and sandboxed workflow evaluation rather than scoring model QA alone (Bilal et al., arXiv:2605.12729). We used these bodies of work to select a deterministic verification oracle design, establish canonical task templates, and define paired, within‑task inference as the strictest test consistent with the GVR hypothesis.
sections.methodology: Preregistration: The experimental plan (CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001) and all selection rules were frozen before observation. Tasks & sampling: deterministic stratified sampling (seed 2026‑08‑25) drew 300 device‑level tasks from public canonical templates: routing=150, ACL=100, BGP=50. Inclusion/exclusion rules, failure treatment, power calculations, multiplicity controls, and contamination checks were preregistered and implemented deterministically. Model & prompts: proposer model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API); the initial master prompt and all prompt templates are archived (see Disclosure). Intervention arms: baseline = single LLM proposal per task; guarded = same initial generation but proposals are passed to a deterministic network verifier that (a) rejects proposals that induce policy or reachability violations in the sandbox model and (b) returns typed counterexamples as repair context; when rejected, the pipeline supplied the verifier diagnostics to the LLM and allowed up to one automated repair call (max repair iterations = 1). Verifier: a deterministic, canonical network verifier (header‑space/reachability style semantics and policy checks) exercised in a deterministic sandbox that simulates the intended device behaviors and evaluates the hypothetical effect of the change (verifier design and test harness archived). Outcomes & estimands: primary endpoint = per‑task binary label 'would‑causing‑unsafe‑state‑if‑applied' (derived from the sandbox simulation); primary estimand = paired absolute reduction in proportion of unsafe proposals (guarded vs baseline) across the N tasks. Analysis plan: preregistered paired McNemar exact tests, 95% exact/Clopper–Pearson CIs, prespecified sensitivity analyses (failed calls, contamination inclusion), and exploratory regression diagnostics. Execution provenance: all model calls, verifier traces, scoring artifacts, and content hashes are preserved (see execution manifest).
sections.results: Execution summary: run completed autonomously (start 2026‑08‑25T12:11:03Z; end 2026‑08‑25T12:51:37Z). Episodes: planned=600 (300 paired tasks × 2 conditions); completed=600; model calls used=301 (300 initial + 1 repair invocation). Confirmatory (preregistered) results: complete paired N=300. Baseline arm: 1 task labeled 'unsafe if applied' (1/300 = 0.33%). Guarded (verifier‑gated GVR) arm: 0 tasks labeled unsafe (0/300 = 0.00%). Paired counts (per preregistered 2×2): n11 (safe in both) = 299; n10 (safe baseline, unsafe guarded) = 1; n01 (unsafe baseline, safe guarded) = 0; n00 (unsafe in both) = 0. Paired absolute risk reduction (guarded − baseline) = +0.00333 (favoring guarded); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Bootstrap 95% CI for paired difference: [0.00, 0.01] (paired bootstrap percentile, 10k resamples, seed=1729). Interpretation (confirmatory): the observable numeric reduction is small (1→0) and does not meet the preregistered target effect (≥50% relative reduction) nor reach statistical significance under the planned test. Exploratory diagnostics: (i) the single discordant case was a baseline proposal whose change pattern included an omitted conditional statement; when the guarded verifier returned a precise counterexample the repair invocation produced a corrected patch that the sandbox accepted; (ii) verifier coverage: remaining theoretical failure surfaces concentrate on finely coupled reachability + higher‑level policy constraints that were intentionally out of scope of the verifier model; (iii) contamination checks (hash comparisons vs pre‑lock artifacts) flagged no items; all raw outputs, verifier traces, and scoring JSONs are archived with cryptographic hashes in the execution manifest. Secondary and exploratory analyses (logistic regressions, per‑task family breakouts) are reported in the archived analysis artifacts; no secondary contrast produced strong evidence for larger effects given the sparse failure counts.
sections.discussion: Main finding: for the canonical, deterministic sandbox tasks and the tested LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), proposals were largely safe under the chosen templates (1/300 unsafe at baseline), and interposing a deterministic verifier plus a single repair iteration eliminated the observed unsafe case (1→0) but did not yield a statistically significant confirmatory effect for the preregistered target. Operationally, two implications follow: (1) GVR can be effective in eliminating individual verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals (the discordant case was remediated by the repair loop), and (2) if the production task distribution already produces very low unsafe rates for canonical changes, very large N or higher‑risk task designs are required to measure sizable relative gains. Practical interpretation: a verifier‑gated architecture remains a prudent safety pattern (defense‑in‑depth and auditability), but claims about large absolute improvements must be tied to realistic failure priors and richer task distributions. Limitations and threats to validity (summarized below) constrain generalisability: single model, synthetic canonical tasks, verifier scope, sandbox abstraction, and the paired design’s dependence on deterministic templates. Future work: test higher‑risk, production‑representative changes; evaluate stronger repair search budgets and multi‑agent orchestration; expand verifier expressiveness (policy and stateful device models); and measure operator workload and false‑positive costs in human‑in‑the‑loop settings.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, end‑to‑end autonomous experiment comparing LLM‑only proposals against a deterministic‑verifier‑gated GVR pipeline on 300 canonical NetOps tasks. Observed baseline unsafe proposals were rare (1/300) and the guarded GVR arm eliminated that single unsafe case; however, the absolute effect was small and did not meet the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target or produce a statistically significant paired contrast under the planned test. The result does not falsify GVR as an operational safety pattern—indeed, the repair closed the one observed failure—but it highlights that realistic task selection and verifier coverage are critical when evaluating safety interventions and that small failure rates require much larger samples to demonstrate substantial relative improvements. All code, prompts, raw outputs, verifier diagnostics, scoring artifacts, and hashes are archived to enable reproducible follow‑on studies.

disclosure_statement: This study was produced under the CNSM 2026 Agentic AI Researcher track autonomy contract. Post‑lock autonomy boundary and human role: the Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and approved the autonomy boundary before the autonomous run. After the autonomy lock, the AI system autonomously performed literature discovery, research‑gap selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting. Models and tools used (archived): proposer model = gpt‑5‑mini (hosted API provider; exact provider call logs and call cache are archived), orchestration/adapter framework = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 (adapter and execution harness code archived), deterministic verifier = canonical header‑space/reachability‑style verifier implemented for the sandbox (implementation archived). Exact master prompt and all task‑level prompt templates were preserved and hashed; a machine‑readable copy of the initial master prompt (the frozen master prompt and its ID) is included in the archived preregistration artifact (study id CNSM2026‑GVR‑BATFISH‑CAND‑001). The Research Director constrained the scientific scope to "reliability, safety, validation, correctness, robustness, or operational trustworthiness of LLM‑ or agent‑generated NetOps actions" before lock. The experiment was preregistered (frozen) prior to any data collection; the preregistration document and its SHA‑256 hash are archived in the execution manifest. Execution logging: all model calls, provider responses, verifier traces, repair prompts, parsed canonical configs, raw outputs, scoring artifacts, and provenance hashes were recorded and archived (see execution_manifest and analysis artifacts). Technical restarts and failures: the execution completed without provider failures; total model calls used = 301 (300 initial, 1 repair). No human manually edited experiment outputs, analyses, or manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development: prior infrastructure development and rehearsals occurred but were explicitly excluded from the confirmatory evidence set; contamination checks used deterministic hash comparisons and flagged no pre‑lock artifacts in the confirmatory set. Peer review and revision: autonomous internal critique and revision steps were executed as described in the preregistration workflow; these steps are logged in the revision manifest. Limitations of disclosed components: model identifier is gpt‑5‑mini as used via a hosted API (exact provider endpoint and credentials are not published for security and provider‑terms reasons), and the verifier is a sandbox model (deterministic for reproducibility) that abstracts vendor‑specific implementation details. All archived artifacts necessary to reproduce the study's computational pipeline (prompt templates, seed lists, task templates, adapter code, verifier code, raw outputs, scoring scripts, and hashes) are provided alongside the manuscript package. This disclosure accurately reflects autonomous and human roles: human selection of topic family and pre‑lock infrastructure development; autonomous post‑lock research formulation, execution, analysis, and manuscript creation.
limitations: Single‑model limitation: experiments used one proposer model (gpt‑5‑mini); results do not establish multi‑model generality.
Synthetic/canonical task set: tasks were deterministic canonical templates (routing/ACL/BGP); production change distributions may have higher base failure rates.
Verifier scope: the deterministic verifier modeled a canonical subset of device semantics and policy checks; some coupled reachability+policy failure modes lie outside its coverage.

Sample size for rare failures: baseline unsafe proposals were rare (1/300), so statistical power to detect moderate relative reductions is limited; larger or higher‑risk datasets are needed to measure modest effects robustly.
Sandbox abstraction: sandbox simulation approximates device semantics and does not substitute for vendor‑specific, device‑level execution in production.
Repair budget limited: the pipeline allowed only one automated repair iteration per preregistration; alternate repair search budgets or multi‑agent repair strategies were not evaluated here.
